topics: 🗣️ Cursing Another With God's Name — the 'warning' verse from 'do not curse the deaf'
🧺 Teruma Before Bikkurim — a three-way identity puzzle solved via a Demai mishna
🔄 Lavin That Can Be Rectified — why such prohibitions usually carry no lashes
🐐 Temurah's Exception — two prohibitions and only one positive mitzva

❓ Abaye vs. Rava — does a forbidden act still 'take effect'?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Rectifiable Prohibitions and Temurah's Exception
overview.subtitle: Temurah 4a–4b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the discussion of cursing another with God's name, then untangles which of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina ruled that separating teruma before bikkurim (first fruits) carries lashes, using a parallel dispute about tithing baskets out of order. Rabbi Avin explains the exemption: it is a prohibition 'that can be rectified' by a later positive mitzva (לָאו שֶׁנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה), and such prohibitions normally carry no lashes. Abaye challenges this from temurah itself, which is also rectifiable yet does carry lashes — resolved because temurah involves two prohibitions with only one positive mitzva to rectify them. The daf closes with a broader tannaitic dispute about the Paschal offering's leftover meat, and Abaye and Rava's fundamental question: when the Torah forbids an act, does the act still take effect if performed anyway?

slides.title: 🗣️ Two Verses Needed: Prohibition and Warning
slides.subtitle: A punishable prohibition requires both an issur and a distinct azhara (warning of punishment)
rows: Deuteronomy 28:59, 'the Lord will make your plagues wondrous'
"You shall not curse the deaf" (Leviticus 19:14) — a separate verse
Would need the same verse as above
None available — "You shall fear the Lord" (Deut. 6:13) is a positive command, which cannot serve as a warning

callout.label: Conclusion:
callout.text: Because a warning verse exists for cursing another but not for uttering the Name in vain, Deuteronomy 28:59 must be referring to the former, not the latter.

slides.title: 🧺 Who Says Teruma-Before-Bikkurim Is Flogged?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina disagree; the Gemara identifies each side

nodes.content: ❓ One of the two says 'lokeh', the other 'eino lokeh' — but which is which?
📖 Parallel case (Mishna Demai): two baskets of untithed produce; 'the tithe of this is in that, and that is in this' — first basket tithed, second not
⚖️ Rabbi Elazar there rules: flogged, for separating second tithe before first tithe (wrong order)
✅ Therefore Rabbi Elazar is the one who holds teruma-before-bikkurim is flogged; Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina holds it is not

callout.label: Resolving the earlier attribution:
callout.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina's earlier statement (3a) about 'the one who advances teruma' must then be read as referring to the exemption, not the punishment.

slides.title: 🔄 Two Reasons a Prohibition Might Carry No Lashes
slides.subtitle: The Gemara distinguishes two independent grounds for exemption

boxes.title: לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה
items: A prohibition violated with no physical action at all

boxes.title: לָאו שֶׁנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה
items: A prohibition the Torah pairs with a later positive mitzva that rectifies it
General rule: no lashes (Rabbi Avin, from 'out of all your tithes you shall set apart')
Example: teruma before bikkurim — one must still separate the fruits afterward

callout.label: Why this matters for temurah:
callout.text: Substitution also involves an act rectifiable by a positive mitzva ('both it and its substitute shall be holy'), yet the mishna flogs the substituter — an apparent exception that needs its own explanation.

slides.title: 🐐 Why Temurah Still Gets Lashes
slides.subtitle: Rav Dimi answers Abaye's challenge, then meets a counter-challenge from the case of the rapist

steps.content: 1️⃣ Abaye to Rav Dimi: if 'rectifiable' prohibitions carry no lashes, why is the temurah-substituter flogged? Temurah too is rectified by 'both shall be holy'!
2️⃣ Rav Dimi: the verse states two prohibitions — 'he shall not exchange it... nor substitute it' — but only one positive mitzva to rectify. One positive mitzva cannot uproot two prohibitions
3️⃣ Challenge from the rapist (ones): one prohibition ('he may not send her away'), one positive mitzva ('she shall be his wife') — yet a priest who divorces his victim is still flogged!
4️⃣ Resolved: a priest's case is different for an unrelated reason — the Torah increased the severity of priestly prohibitions due to their greater holiness

callout.label: Net result:
callout.text: Rectifiable prohibitions are normally lash-free, but exceptions exist for their own structural reasons — two prohibitions for one remedy (temurah), or heightened priestly sanctity (the rapist-priest).

slides.title: ❓ Does a Forbidden Act Still 'Take Effect'?
slides.subtitle: Abaye and Rava dispute the deeper logic behind all these lashes

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Whenever the Merciful One says 'do not do this,' if one did it anyway, the act takes effect. If it didn't take effect, why would he be flogged for accomplishing nothing?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: No — the act accomplishes nothing at all. He is flogged simply because he transgressed the word of the Merciful One, regardless of whether anything actually happened.

callout.label: Big idea:
callout.text: This dispute frames the whole tractate's puzzle: temurah is the clearest case where a forbidden act (Abaye's view) plainly does take effect — the animal becomes consecrated even though the act itself is punished.

summary.principle: Most prohibitions rectifiable by a later positive mitzva carry no lashes, but temurah is a structural exception — two prohibitions matched to only one remedy — which is why substitution is flogged even though it 'succeeds.'

flowSteps.content: 🗣️ Cursing another needs its own warning verse; 'name in vain' has none (a positive mitzva can't serve)
🧺 Rabbi Elazar (flogged) vs. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina (not) on teruma before bikkurim, resolved via the Demai baskets

columns.content: 🔄 Rectifiable prohibitions (lav sheanitak la'aseh) usually get no lashes
🐐 Temurah: two lavin, one aseh — the exception

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Abaye — a forbidden act still takes effect; Rava — lashes come from the transgression alone

quiz.q: Why can Deuteronomy 28:59 ('the Lord will make your plagues wondrous') not be referring to pronouncing God's name in vain?
o: Because that sin carries no punishment at all
Because no separate warning (azhara) verse exists for it — 'you shall fear the Lord' is a positive command and cannot serve as a warning
Because only priests can transgress it
Because it only applies to gentiles
quiz.e: A punishable prohibition needs both a prohibition and a distinct warning verse; cursing another has 'you shall not curse the deaf' as its warning, but pronouncing the Name in vain has no such prohibition-phrased verse available.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara determine that Rabbi Elazar (not Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina) holds that separating teruma before bikkurim incurs lashes?
o: By a direct quote where he says so explicitly
By comparing it to his ruling in the Demai mishna that separating tithes out of order is flogged
By elimination, since only two opinions exist
Because he was a priest
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar's ruling about the two baskets of tevel — that flogging applies for separating second tithe before first tithe (wrong order) — parallels teruma-before-bikkurim, identifying him as the one who says it is flogged.

quiz.q: What does 'לָאו שֶׁנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה' (a prohibition that can be rectified) mean, and what is its normal legal consequence?
o: A prohibition with no possible violation; no consequence
A prohibition paired with a later positive mitzva that corrects the violation; normally, no lashes
A prohibition unique to the Temple; always flogged
A prohibition that applies only to women
quiz.e: When the Torah attaches a positive mitzva to rectify a prohibition's violation (like separating the earlier tithe after the later one), the transgressor is normally exempt from lashes.

quiz.q: How does Rav Dimi explain why the temurah-substituter is flogged despite temurah being rectifiable by 'both shall be holy'?
o: Temurah isn't actually rectifiable
The verse contains two separate prohibitions but only one positive mitzva, and one mitzva cannot uproot two prohibitions
Temurah only applies to animals, not produce
Rav Dimi says he actually is not flogged
quiz.e: Rav Dimi notes the verse states both 'he shall not exchange it' and 'nor substitute it' — two prohibitions — while only one positive mitzva ('both shall be holy') exists to rectify them, so the rule doesn't apply.

quiz.q: What is the core dispute between Abaye and Rava about a forbidden act performed anyway?
o: Abaye says it never takes effect; Rava says it always does
Abaye says the act takes effect (hence the lashes make sense); Rava says it accomplishes nothing, and lashes come purely from transgressing God's word
They agree entirely and merely phrase it differently
The dispute concerns only monetary law, not sacrifices
quiz.e: Abaye reasons that lashes for an ineffective act would be pointless, so the act must take effect; Rava holds the act is void, and the lashes punish the transgression itself, regardless of any resulting effect.
